items.stem: What is meant by “far point of eye”?
items.answer: The maximum distance from the eye upto which the eye can see an object clearly is called the far point of the eye. It is infinity for a normal eye.

items.stem: What is meant by near point of a human eye?
items.answer: By near point of a human eye, we mean the nearest position of an object from a human eye so that its sharp image is formed on the retina. It is 25 cm for a person with normal vision.

items.stem: Why can a chicken see only in bright light? Explain.
items.answer: A chicken has mostly cone cells on the retina of its eye which respond to bright light. This is why a chicken can see only in bright light.
items.ocr: Printed question mark was missing after “bright light”; restored from the printed “Explain.”

items.stem: How do we see colours?
items.answer: There are rod and cone cells present on the retina. Among cone cells some respond to red colour, some to blue colour and some to green colour. Due to different colours of light these cells become active and help in perception of colours.

items.stem: Write the role of the following parts of an eye: (a) Pupil, (b) Retina, (c) Optic nerve.
items.answer: (a) Pupil: The amount of light is controlled by the size of the pupil. In dim light, it opens completely and in bright light, it becomes very small. (b) Retina: Retina is a light sensitive surface of the eye where the real image is formed. (c) Optic nerve: It carries the electrical signals from the light sensitive eye cells to the brain.
items.ocr: The label “(c)” before “Optic nerve” was lost in the printed answer; restored from the question's own list.

items.stem: State in brief the functions of the following parts of the human eye: (a) Iris (b) Cornea (c) Ciliary muscles (d) Pupil.
items.answer: (a) Iris: It controls the size of the pupil. (b) Cornea: It acts as a protective layer and is responsible for maximum refraction of light that enters the eye. (c) Ciliary muscles: They help in adjusting the focal length of the eye-lens. (d) Pupil: It regulates and controls the amount of light entering the eye.
items.ocr: A bare “NODIA” watermark sat inside the answer between (a) and (b) and was stripped. The printed answer lists Pupil before Ciliary muscles; re-ordered to match the question's (a)-(d) labels.

items.stem: Why does it take some time to see the objects in a dim-lit room when we enter the room from bright sunlight outside? OR Why does it take some time to see objects in a cinema hall when we just enter the hall from bright sunlight? Explain in brief.
items.answer: In bright light, the size of the pupil is small to control the amount of light entering the eye. When we enter a dim-lit room or a cinema hall, it takes some time so that the pupil expands and allows more light to enter the eye and thus helps to see things clearly.

items.stem: (a) What is meant by least distance of distinct vision? (b) How does the thickness of the eye lens change when we shift from looking at a distant tree to reading a book?
items.answer: (a) The minimum distance of an object from the eye at which the image of the object is seen clearly is called the least distance of distinct vision. It is 25 cm for a healthy person. (b) The eye lens becomes comparatively thicker while reading a book.

items.stem: What is cataract?
items.answer: Due to the development of a membrane over the eye lens, the eye becomes ineffective or the image becomes hazy. This problem is called cataract.

items.stem: What do you mean by dispersion of light? What is its cause?
items.answer: When white light is passed through a glass prism, it splits into its seven constituent colours (VIBGYOR). This phenomenon is called dispersion. Cause of dispersion: Light rays of different colours (or different wavelengths) travel at the same speed in vacuum or air. However, they travel with different speeds in a refractive medium like glass. The violet coloured ray travels with the least speed and the red ray with the maximum speed. Thus the refractive index of glass for violet colour is maximum and that for red is minimum. As a result, the different coloured rays bend differently on entering glass. The violet ray is deviated the most and the red the least, giving rise to the dispersion phenomenon.

items.stem: Draw a neat diagram to show the refraction of a light ray through a glass prism and label on it the angle of incidence and angle of deviation.
items.answer: In the ray diagram of a triangular glass prism: PE – Incident ray, ∠i – Angle of incidence, EF – Refracted ray, ∠r – Angle of refraction, FS – Emergent ray, ∠e – Angle of emergence, ∠A – Angle of the prism, ∠D – Angle of deviation. The ray bends towards the base of the prism on entering and again on leaving it, so the emergent ray FS is deviated from the direction of the incident ray PE by the angle of deviation ∠D.
items.ocr: MinerU rendered the legend's angle symbols as bare “+” signs ($\angle$ lost): restored ∠i, ∠e, ∠A, ∠D from context. The figure on p14 belongs to the worked solution (the student must draw it), so it is not attached.

items.stem: What is angle of deviation?
items.answer: When a monochromatic ray is passed through a prism it emerges finally bent towards the base of the prism. The angle between the direction of the incident ray and the direction of the emergent ray is called the angle of deviation.

items.stem: Which component of white light deviates (i) the least and (ii) the most while passing through a glass prism? State the reason for this difference in deviation.
items.answer: (i) Least: Red. (ii) Most: Violet. Reason: Due to the variation in their wavelengths and the difference in the refractive indices of the medium for them, the difference in deviation takes place.

items.stem: (i) What happens to a narrow beam of white light when it passes through a glass prism? (ii) Draw a labelled diagram to illustrate it.
items.answer: (i) When a narrow beam of white light passes through a glass prism, dispersion of white light takes place. The white light splits into its seven constituent colours, which is known as a spectrum. (ii) Diagram: the white beam entering the prism emerges as a band of colours from red (deviated least) at the top to violet (deviated most) at the bottom, caught on a screen as the spectrum VIBGYOR.
items.ocr: The p14 spectrum figure is the answer diagram the student is asked to draw, so it is not attached to the question.

items.stem: How did Newton show that white light of the Sun contains seven colours using two prisms? Draw a ray diagram when two prisms are arranged together.
items.answer: Newton placed two identical but inverted prisms together and passed a beam of white light through the first prism. After emerging from it the white beam gave seven different colours. These colours, when they emerged after passing through the second (inverted) prism, got united to give a single white beam of light.
items.ocr: The p14 two-prism figure belongs to the worked solution, so it is not attached.

items.stem: (i) Why do parallel rays of different colours deviate differently while passing through a glass prism? (ii) Name any two phenomena associated with the formation of a rainbow.
items.answer: (i) Parallel rays of different colours deviate differently while passing through a glass prism because the angles of refraction for different colours are different (the refractive index of glass differs for each colour). (ii) Two phenomena associated with the formation of a rainbow are: (a) Dispersion of sunlight by water droplets present in the atmosphere, and (b) Total internal reflection.
items.ocr: Answer was split by the column jumble: part (i) ends on p14 with a “Click Here to Buy book on Amazon” banner (stripped) and part (ii) resumes at the top of the p17 block; the two halves were rejoined here.

items.stem: Describe the formation of rainbow in the sky with the help of a diagram.
items.answer: A rainbow is always formed in a direction opposite to that of the Sun. The water droplets act like small prisms. They refract and disperse the incident sunlight, then reflect it internally, and finally refract it again when it comes out of the droplet. Due to the dispersion of light and internal reflection, different colours reach the observer's eye.
items.ocr: The p17 rainbow figure is the answer diagram, so it is not attached. Printed solution's closing words read “internal refraction”; the physics and its own earlier sentence give internal reflection.

items.stem: (i) Show the formation of rainbow with the help of a ray diagram. (ii) What are the conditions to observe a rainbow?
items.answer: (i) Formation of rainbow: sunlight entering a raindrop is refracted and dispersed, totally internally reflected at the back surface of the drop, and refracted again as it leaves, so the colours emerge spread out and reach the observer's eye. (ii) One can observe a rainbow if the Sun shines at the back of the observer during or after rainfall.
items.ocr: The p17 figure belongs to the worked solution (the student is asked to draw it), so it is not attached.

items.stem: (i) When white light is incident on a glass prism surface, it splits into constituent colours. Why? (ii) Write the colours in the order as they appear in the spectrum. (iii) Draw a ray diagram to show dispersion of white light as it passes through a glass prism.
items.answer: (i) The speed of light in a medium depends upon its wavelength. Light of red colour has the longest wavelength while light of violet colour has the shortest wavelength. Therefore, different colours are refracted by different amounts. This is the reason why, when a ray of white light passes through a prism, splitting takes place. (ii) Red, Orange, Yellow, Green, Blue, Indigo and Violet (ROYGBIV, or VIBGYOR read the other way). (iii) Ray diagram: white light incident on one face of the prism emerges from the other face as a band of seven colours, violet deviated most and red least.
items.ocr: The p17 dispersion figure is the answer diagram, so it is not attached.

items.stem: A beam of white light falling on a glass prism gets split up into seven colours, marked 1 to 7 in the figure, reading from the top. A student makes the following statements. (a) The colours at positions marked 1 and 3 are similar to the colour of ‘turmeric’ and the colour of ‘chilli powder’ respectively. Is the above statement correct or incorrect? Justify. (b) Which two positions correspond to the colour of a solution of copper sulphate and the signal used to move vehicles? (c) Light of the colour of chilli powder bends the most while the light of the colour of brinjal bends the least. Is the statement correct? Justify.
items.answer: (a) Incorrect. Position 3 is turmeric (yellow) and position 1 is chilli powder (red), i.e. the two are interchanged. (b) The colour of a solution of copper sulphate is blue, which is at position 5, while the signal used to move vehicles is green in colour, which is at position 4. (c) Incorrect. Violet (the colour of brinjal) bends the most and red (the colour of chilli powder) bends the least.
items.ocr: Figure attached: the question depends on the numbered spectrum positions and the p17 figure sits with the question text, before “Ans”. Answer part (c) was displaced by the column jumble to the tail of the p15 block and was rejoined here. Added “marked 1 to 7 in the figure” to the stem since the printed stem relies on the figure's labels.

items.stem: A star appears on the horizon. What is the true position of the star? Explain with the help of a diagram.
items.answer: The true position of the star is below the horizon. Incident rays from the star travel through the earth's atmosphere and reach the observer's eye. These incident rays travel from the rarer atmosphere to the denser atmosphere and bend towards the normal. Thus, they appear to come from a different position which is slightly upwards, so the star is seen above its true position.
items.ocr: The p16 figure belongs to the worked solution, so it is not attached.

items.stem: What is the scattering of light? Explain with the help of an example.
items.answer: The phenomenon of change in the direction of propagation of light caused by the large number of particles present in the atmosphere is called scattering of light. Example: The path of a beam of light becomes visible through a colloidal solution due to scattering of light.

items.stem: Why does the clear sky appear blue? OR Why does the colour of the sky appear blue? Explain in brief. OR Why does the sky look blue on a clear sunny day?
items.answer: The molecules of air and other fine particles in the atmosphere have a smaller size than the wavelength of visible light. These are more effective in scattering light of shorter wavelengths at the blue end than light of longer wavelength at the red end. Thus, the blue colour of the sky is due to the scattering of sunlight by fine particles in air.

items.stem: Give reason: (a) Danger signals are red. (b) We cannot see an object clearly if it is placed very close to the eyes.
items.answer: (a) As red colour has the longest wavelength, it scatters the least. As a result, it reaches the eye easily and is visible from the greatest distance. So, danger signals are made red in colour. (b) The least distance of distinct vision is 25 cm. So, an object kept closer than this cannot be seen clearly.

items.stem: Name the phenomenon associated with the following: (a) The sky appears blue. (b) Formation of a rainbow in the sky. (c) Twinkling of stars.
items.answer: (a) (i) Atmospheric refraction. (ii) Scattering of blue colour (Tyndall effect). (b) (i) Dispersion. (ii) Total internal reflection. (iii) Refraction. (c) (i) Atmospheric refraction. (ii) Change in the density of the atmosphere due to temperature and other conditions.
items.ocr: Printed answer (b) reads “Internal reflection”; expanded to total internal reflection to match the same book's answer to Q96(ii).

items.stem: A person is not able to see distinctly the objects placed beyond 90 cm from him. Giving reasons, identify the defect in his eye. Determine the nature of lens used to correct this defect.
items.answer: It is because the image of a distant object is formed in front of the retina and not at the retina itself. The defect in his eye is myopia. A concave lens is used to bring the image back onto the retina and thus the defect is corrected.

items.stem: A student sitting at the back seat of a class is not able to see what is written on the blackboard. He however sees it clearly when sitting on the front seat at an approximate distance of 1.5 m from the blackboard. Draw ray diagrams to illustrate the image formation of the blackboard writing by his eye-lens when he is seated at the (i) back seat (ii) front seat.
items.answer: He is suffering from myopia. (i) When he is seated at the back seat, rays from the distant blackboard are converged by his eye-lens to form the image in front of the retina, so the writing looks blurred. (ii) When he is seated at the front seat, the object is near enough that his eye-lens forms the image exactly on the retina, so the writing is seen clearly.
items.ocr: Column jumble: the two answer ray diagrams print on p15 while the question text prints on p16, and the printed answer text is only the two captions “When he is seated at the back seat / front seat”. Both figures belong to the worked solution, so they are not attached.

items.stem: Name the part of the eye where the image is formed in a normal human eye. State how the image position changes in myopia and hypermetropia.
items.answer: Retina. In myopia the image of a distant object falls in front of the retina, and a concave lens brings the image back onto the retina; in hypermetropia the image of a nearby object falls behind the retina, and a convex lens brings the image onto the retina.

items.stem: Why is there no dispersion of light refracted through a rectangular glass slab?
items.answer: After refraction at the two parallel faces of a glass slab, a ray of light emerges in a direction parallel to the direction of incidence of the white light. As rays of all colours emerge in the same direction, i.e. the direction of incidence of the white light, there is no dispersion. However, there is lateral displacement.

items.stem: Why is it difficult to drive on a foggy day?
items.answer: On a foggy day, most of the light gets scattered by the particles in the fog and the visibility reduces, so it is difficult and dangerous to drive on a foggy day.

items.stem: Mention the factor on which scattering of light depends. Why does the sky appear dark in space?
items.answer: It depends on the presence of an atmosphere containing smoke particles, tiny water droplets, suspended particles of dust and molecules of air (and on the size of these particles relative to the wavelength of light). When a beam of light strikes such fine particles, the path of the beam becomes visible. The sky appears dark in space because there are no air molecules there to scatter light.

items.stem: How can change of size of the eye-ball be one of the reasons for (a) a myopic eye (b) a hypermetropic eye?
items.answer: (a) Myopic eye: The eye ball is longer than normal, due to which the image formed by the eye lens lies in front of the retina. (b) Hypermetropic eye: The eye ball is shorter than normal, due to which the image formed by the eye lens lies behind the retina.

items.stem: What type of spectacles should be worn by a person having the defects of myopia as well as hypermetropia? How does it help?
items.answer: A person suffering from myopia as well as hypermetropia uses spectacles having bi-focal lenses, in which the upper part consists of a concave lens (to correct myopia) used for distant vision and the lower part consists of a convex lens (to correct hypermetropia) used for reading purposes.

items.stem: Seema prefers to sit in the front row as she finds it difficult to read the black board from the last desk of her class room. State the defect of vision she is suffering from. How is this defect corrected?
items.answer: Seema is suffering from myopia (short-sightedness). She must use concave lenses of appropriate power to correct the defect.

items.stem: No rainbow could be observed from the surface of the moon by the astronauts. Give reason.
items.answer: The moon does not have any blanket of air or atmosphere and consequently, in the absence of water droplets, no dispersion of the sun's rays is possible. Therefore, a rainbow could not be observed from the surface of the moon by the astronauts.

items.stem: What is meant by near point and far point of an eye? State their values for the normal human eye.
items.answer: The nearest point to the eye at which an object is visible distinctly is called the near point (25 cm for a normal eye). The maximum distance up to which the normal eye can see things clearly is called the far point (infinity).

items.stem: What would the sky look like if the earth had no atmosphere? Why?
items.answer: If the earth had no atmosphere consisting of air, there would have been no scattering of sunlight at all. In that case no light from the sky would have entered our eyes and the sky would have looked dark and black to us.
items.ocr: Answer was broken by the column jumble: it breaks off mid-sentence at “no scattering of sunlight at” on p15 (with Q100's answer part (c) intruding) and resumes with “all. In that case...” at the top of the p18 block; the halves were rejoined.

items.stem: A student uses spectacles of focal length –60 cm. Name the defect of vision he is suffering from. Which lens is used for the correction of this defect? Compute the power of this lens.
items.answer: The student is suffering from the myopia defect. A diverging (concave) lens is used for the correction of this defect. Power of the lens, P = 1/f(in m) = 100/f(in cm) = 100/(−60) = −1.67 D.

items.stem: Draw a neat labelled diagram of the human eye.
items.answer: The labelled diagram of the human eye shows the cornea, aqueous humour, iris, pupil, crystalline eye lens, ciliary muscles, vitreous humour, retina, optic nerve, sclera (sclerotic) and the blind spot, with light entering through the cornea and the inverted real image forming on the retina.

items.stem: Why does it take some time to see objects in a cinema hall when we just enter the hall from bright sunlight? Explain.
items.answer: The pupil regulates and controls the amount of light entering the eye. In bright sunlight, the size of the pupil is small, and when we enter the cinema hall it takes some time for the pupil to expand in size due to the dim light.

items.stem: The far point of a myopic person is 80 cm in front of the eyes. What is the nature and power of the lens required to enable him to see very distant objects clearly?
items.answer: For a myopic eye the correcting lens is concave. Distance of far point, x = 80 cm. For viewing distant objects the focal length of the corrective lens is f = −x = −80 cm. Now power, P = 1/f(in m) = 100/f(in cm) = 100/(−80) = −1.25 D. So a concave lens of power −1.25 D is required.
items.ocr: LaTeX rewritten to Unicode: “$x = 8 0 \mathrm{cm}$” → x = 80 cm, and the displayed array for f and P set inline. No year tag was printed for this question.

items.stem: A glass prism is able to produce a spectrum when white light passes through it but a glass slab does not produce any spectrum. Explain why it is so.
items.answer: When white light enters the glass slab, dispersion of light does take place: violet colour is refracted (bent) more than red colour on entering the glass slab. But all colours of light return to the original direction of propagation on refraction at the other, parallel face of the glass slab, and thus white light emerges out of the glass slab. Hence, a glass slab does not produce any spectrum, while a prism, whose faces are inclined, does.
items.ocr: Printed stem's duplicated tail “Explain. Why it is so ?” merged into one sentence. The printed solution reads “the angle of refraction for violet colour is more than for red colour”, which is false as written — violet has the larger refractive index, so its angle of refraction is smaller than red's; rewritten as violet being refracted (bent) more, which is the book's evident intent.
